2.1.4.2-r10.burton_quote: because the parties are so restless, and impatient

2.1.4.2-r11.burton_quote: to take physic, not for a month, a year, but to apply himself to their prescriptions all the days of his life

2.1.4.2-r12.burton_quote: that without exquisite knowledge, to work out of books is most dangerous: how unsavoury a thing it is to believe Writers, and take upon trust, as this patient perceived by his own peril

2.1.4.2-r2.burton_quote: all the gold they had, if all the city were gold he should have it

2.1.4.2-r3.burton_quote: to be more troublesome to their Physicians, than other ordinary patients, that they may have change of physic

2.1.4.2-r4.burton_quote: confidence and hope do more good than physic

2.1.4.2-r5.burton_quote: why Hippocrates was so fortunate in his cures, not for any extraordinary skill he had; but because the common people had a most strong conceit of his worth

2.1.4.2-r6.burton_quote: that he should not alter his Physician, or prescribed physic: nothing hinders health more; a wound can never be cured that hath several plasters

2.1.4.2-r7.burton_quote: ’Tis proper to them, if things fall not out to their mind, and that they have not present ease, to seek another, and another (as they do commonly that have sore eyes); twenty, one after another, and they still promise all to cure them

2.1.4.2-r8.burton_quote: perseverance and sufferance, for in such a small time no great matter can be effected

2.1.4.2-r9.burton_quote: if she will be cured, she must be of a most abiding patience, faithful obedience, and singular perseverance; if she remit, or despair, she can expect or hope for no good success
